title: The Sleepless Brain's Doughnut Problem
description: This episode examines a study on sleep-deprived adults showing that missing a full night of sleep shifts brain activity, dampening regions involved in weighing choices while boosting regions tied to salience, making high calorie food more appealing. It also notes the limits of this evidence, since it comes from one small study of total sleep loss rather than the partial sleep loss most people actually experience.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: After a bad night’s sleep, something strange can happen. The doughnut you ignored yesterday suddenly looks like a very good idea, while the salad feels more like a chore. We usually call that a lack of willpower. But does losing sleep actually change what your brain wants to eat, or are you simply too tired to resist? In 2013, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, put 23 healthy adults through two conditions: one night of normal sleep, and another where they were kept awake for the entire night. The next day, the participants had their brains scanned while they looked at pictures of different foods, from fruit and vegetables to burgers, pizza and sweets, and rated how much they wanted each one. After the sleepless night, several areas toward the front of the brain involved in evaluating choices, assigning value and helping regulate behaviour became less responsive to the food. At the same time, the amygdala became more active. The amygdala is involved in detecting things that are emotionally important or particularly salient — essentially, things that grab your attention and tell your brain, “Pay attention to this.” So the researchers were seeing an interesting shift: areas involved in carefully evaluating the choice became quieter, while a system involved in flagging things as important became louder.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: And that difference showed up in what people actually wanted. After a completely sleepless night, participants rated high-calorie foods as more desirable, with the researchers estimating roughly 600 additional calories' worth of high-calorie foods being selected as desirable compared with the rested condition. Their interest in low-calorie foods barely changed. But here's the part that makes the result particularly interesting: the participants did not report being significantly hungrier. They weren't simply saying, “I'm starving, give me anything.” Their reported hunger was about the same. What appeared to change was the type of food that looked appealing. The people who felt more impaired and groggy after the sleepless night also tended to show the strongest preference for high-calorie foods. That suggests the effect wasn't simply an empty stomach demanding more food. Something about losing sleep appeared to change how the brain evaluated different food choices — making calorie-dense, highly tempting foods more attractive without producing the same increase in reported hunger.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text:
So the next time you wake up after a terrible night and the biscuits in the cupboard suddenly seem far more interesting than they did yesterday, it may not be entirely a story about willpower. Your brain may genuinely be evaluating those choices differently. The NHS recommends that most adults aim for around seven to nine hours of sleep a night. And after three in the morning, apparently, your kitchen can become a remarkably persuasive place.
